topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Nature of Binary
sections.content: Briefly introduce the binary system (base-2). Explain that just as decimal uses 0-9, binary uses 0 and 1 to represent powers of two. Focus on the concept of 'bit position' representing 2^n.
sections.example: Visualizing a 3-bit counter: 000 (0), 001 (1), 010 (2), 011 (3), 100 (4). Animation: As the binary number increments, a single bit flips at each step.

sections.title: The Towers of Hanoi Rules
sections.content: Define the classic puzzle: 3 rods, n disks of different sizes. Rule 1: Move one disk at a time. Rule 2: Never place a larger disk on a smaller one. Goal: Move the full tower to another rod.
sections.example: A 3-disk stack. An animation shows the illegal move (big disk on small) being blocked by a red 'X', while legal moves are highlighted in green.

sections.title: The Binary Connection
sections.content: Introduce the breakthrough insight: The sequence of disk moves follows the rhythm of a binary counter. In a 3-disk puzzle, the disk to move is determined by the position of the first '1' bit in the binary sequence of steps.
sections.example: Step 1 (001): Move Disk 1. Step 2 (010): Move Disk 2. Step 3 (011): Move Disk 1 again. Animation syncs binary numbers 1-7 on the left with disk movements on the right.

sections.title: Scaling to Complexity
sections.content: Explain why this works: The minimum number of moves is 2^n - 1. Connect this to the binary capacity of n bits. This shows that the puzzle is essentially a physical representation of an n-bit binary counter.
sections.example: A cute robot character attempting the puzzle. If the robot follows the 'binary instruction set' (even for 10 disks), it solves it perfectly without ever checking the rules.

sections.title: Summary & Application
sections.content: Wrap up by emphasizing that complex recursive problems can often be mapped to simple binary patterns. This is the foundation of how computers process logic.
sections.example: Display a final graphic: A 'Binary-Tower Cheat Sheet' where a scroll of paper with binary numbers 001, 010, 011... directly maps to the disk movement instructions.
